title: 5 Leadership Lessons I Learned Managing High Performers
author: The Good Boss
summary: Drawing on two decades of leading engineering and technology teams, the author of The Good Boss identifies five counterintuitive lessons about managing high performers. High performers need context and strategic clarity rather than control -- they want to understand the 'why' and find better solutions when they own the mission. They need recognition more than most leaders realize, because organizations normalize excellence and contributions become invisible. They get bored faster and disengage when work becomes repetitive or political -- and unlike average performers, they have options. They often need 'air cover' from organizational noise rather than more coaching. Finally, 'brilliant jerks' -- highly talented people who create unhealthy team dynamics -- weaken collective performance if tolerated. Sustainable high performance requires trust, collaboration, and collective effectiveness.
points: * High performers resist unnecessary control but thrive with strategic clarity: 'I stopped thinking of management as directing execution and started thinking of it as creating alignment and enabling ownership.' * Recognition matters especially for high performers: organizations 'slowly normalize their excellence,' and the more reliable someone becomes, the less acknowledgment they often receive. * High performers get bored faster than others and have 'options' -- disengagement quickly becomes departure if work becomes repetitive, stagnant, or overly political. * 'Air cover' -- protecting high performers from organizational noise and constant competing demands -- is often more valuable than coaching or direct advice. * 'Brilliant jerks' -- highly talented people who dominate discussions, dismiss teammates, and create intimidating environments -- weaken the team and must be addressed despite their individual output. * Sustainable high performance requires more than individual brilliance: it requires trust, collaboration, and collective effectiveness.
quotes: High performers do not need 'less' leadership. They need a very different kind of leadership.
What they wanted instead was clarity around the larger mission: what problem we were solving, why it mattered, and how success would ultimately be measured.
The more reliable someone becomes, the less recognition they often receive.
One of the greatest gifts a manager can give a high performer is the ability to work deeply on meaningful problems without constant organizational interference.
Sustainable high performance requires more than individual brilliance. It requires trust, collaboration, and collective effectiveness, not individual brilliance.
